title: Respect for suppliants · lines 93–100
subtitle: At Branchidae Aristodicus puts the Cymaeans' dilemma to the god himself

notes.label: Fast pace
notes.trans: when they had arrived at Branchidae
notes.body: A genitive absolute covers the whole journey in four words, so the story moves straight to the question.

notes.label: Delay
notes.body: The singular verb comes first and his name is held back, so the reader sees one man taking over the whole embassy.

notes.label: Juxtaposition
notes.body: "All" is placed right next to the one man, which shows him speaking for the whole city.

notes.label: Direct speech
notes.body: Herodotus switches to direct speech with a respectful address, so the reader hears Aristodicus face to face with the god.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Pactyes' status as a suppliant comes before his name, which puts his religious claim to protection first.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: The key word is repeated, which keeps the god's duty to suppliants in front of him throughout the speech.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The adjective spells out what surrender would mean, which makes the god's answer seem all the harsher.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The Persians come last, at the climax of the sentence, so the reader feels the threat hanging over Pactyes.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Two verbs of command frame the demand, which stresses the pressure the Persians are putting on Cyme.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The Persians are set against the Cymaeans, which presents Cyme as caught in the middle.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.trans: fearing the power of the Persians
notes.body: Aristodicus admits their fear openly, which makes the Cymaeans' dilemma seem honest and sympathetic.

notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: The negative stresses their restraint, which presents the Cymaeans as cautious and pious.

notes.label: Irony
notes.trans: up to now we have not dared
notes.body: The reader knows the Cymaeans were about to hand Pactyes over (line 87), so this claim of careful restraint is ironic.

notes.label: Juxtaposition
notes.body: God and men are placed side by side, which shows that Aristodicus wants an answer straight from the god.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Asking for the answer "exactly" implies the first one was unclear, so the request is really a polite challenge to the god.

notes.label: Deliberative subjunctive
notes.trans: which of the two we are to do
notes.body: The speech ends on a question of what to do, which presents the problem as a simple choice between two options.

questions: Compare Aristodicus' question with the first one in lines 83–84. What has he added, and why?
Is Aristodicus' speech respectful to the god? Find evidence for and against.
What does the word ἀκριβῶς (line 99) suggest Aristodicus thinks about the first answer?

context.body:
Didyma lay on the coast of Asia Minor about 15 kilometres south of Miletus, linked to the city by a sacred road. Its oracle of Apollo was run by the Branchidae, a priestly family who traced their descent from Branchus, a young man loved by the god, and the sanctuary was often called by their name.

It was one of the most respected oracles in the Greek world: Herodotus tells us that Croesus of Lydia sent it rich offerings. When the Ionian cities rebelled against Persia, the Persians took their revenge by plundering and burning the sanctuary (494 BC). The enormous temple whose ruins visitors see today was begun around 300 BC, long after the events of this story.
